title: One road or three?
hook: The straight road to G, or a route with more roads. Which costs less?

knows: spreading out from a start finds the fewest steps (wave-from-the-corner)
doesNotKnow: that with costs on roads the fewest-road route can be the dearest, and how settling the smallest label finds true costs

misconception: The route with the fewest stops is the cheapest.
objective: The learner can settle S, A, B, G in order of smallest label, watch G's first label (10, the straight road) drop to 9, and explain why settling the smallest label first gives true cheapest costs when no cost is negative.

claims.text: With roads S–G 10, S–A 3, S–B 8, A–B 4 and B–G 2, the cheapest cost from S to G is 3 + 4 + 2 = 9 (three roads), and the one-road route costs 10.
claims.source: Demo.tsx runAll(): final labels S 0, A 3, B 7, G 9 (v4 graph). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 24): VERIFIED. Own node Dijkstra on ROADS: final S 0, A 3, B 7, G 9; S-A-B-G = 3+4+2 = 9 (three roads); S-G road 10; S-B-G 10. Matches runAll().

claims.text: Settling S gives A 3, B 8 and G 10; settling A drops B from 8 to 7; settling B drops G from 10 to 9; settling G changes nothing. G's first label is not its final one.
claims.source: Demo.tsx settle() trace on the QA path (S, A, B, G); the message line shows each update and the trace row records G 10 → 9. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 24): VERIFIED. Own node trace of settle(): S gives A 3, B 8, G 10; A: B 8 -> 7; B: G 10 -> 9; G: no changes. Labels never tie, so the tap order is forced (a larger label is refused) and every learner run matches; G history '10 then 9' kept in run after Start again.

claims.text: Settling the smallest label first is safe: with no negative costs, any other way to that town passes a label at least as big, and costs only add, so each settled label is a true cheapest cost. On stage: when A is settled the other open labels are B 8 and G 10; when B is settled, G 10; going from B to A would cost 11, more than A's 3, and from G to B 11, more than B's 7.
claims.source: CLRS (3rd ed.) 24.3, Theorem 24.6 (correctness of Dijkstra's algorithm for non-negative weights). Stage numbers from Demo.tsx tap(): the 'why' line lists the other open labels before the settle; backRoute() gives the later route's cost to a settled town. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 24): VERIFIED. Derivation: with non-negative costs every path to v leaves the settled set through an open town whose label is >= the minimum, so the minimum label is exact (Dijkstra 1959). Stage numbers from own trace: 'why' line at A lists B 8, G 10; at B lists G 10; backRoute at B: B-A 7+4 = 11 > 3; at G: G-B 9+2 = 11 > 7 (prefers non-S target).
E. W. Dijkstra, 'A note on two problems in connexion with graphs', Numerische Mathematik 1, 269-271, 1959.

claims.text: A label is the cheapest cost from S found so far; the sign for infinity means not reached yet. Settling a town means its label is then final.
claims.source: Definition of the tentative distance d[v] (CLRS 24.1, 'shortest-path estimate'). v4: the definition is a fixed line under the map, so it stays after the first tap. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 24): VERIFIED. Legend 'Label: cheapest cost from S found so far. ∞: not reached yet.'; default message 'Tap a town to settle it: its label is then final.'; START labels Infinity render as ∞. Same after Start again.

recall.question: Roads: P–Q costs 7. P–R costs 3 and R–Q costs 3. Settling the smallest label first, what is Q's final label?
recall.why: Settling P gives R 3 and Q 7; settling R (the smaller) drops Q to 3 + 3 = 6, cheaper than the one-road 7.
